timeline.body: British speculator William Knox D'Arcy secured an oil concession covering nearly all of Persia for just £20,000 and a 16% royalty — the deal that would make Iran's resources a Western strategic prize for the next century.
The largest oil strike yet found in the Middle East erupted at Masjed Soleiman in southwest Persia, and within a year the Anglo-Persian Oil Company was incorporated in London to extract it.

Winston Churchill, then First Lord of the Admiralty, convinced Parliament to buy a controlling 51% stake in Anglo-Persian, binding British naval power to Iranian oil and giving London a direct motive to control Tehran's politics.

The CIA and MI6 overthrew Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh after he nationalized the oil industry, installing Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi as a compliant autocrat — an intervention the CIA did not formally acknowledge until 2013.
Israel and Shah-era Iran established deep but quiet security ties under the 'Periphery Doctrine,' with Mossad helping train SAVAK, the Shah's feared secret police.
The Islamic Revolution toppled the Shah, severed all ties with Israel, and turned the US from Iran's closest ally into its primary adversary virtually overnight.

Saddam Hussein invaded Iran with tacit US encouragement, launching an eight-year war that killed roughly 500,000 people — Washington supplied Iraq with satellite intelligence and looked away when Saddam used chemical weapons on Iranian troops.
The GCC was founded in Riyadh, explicitly as a security bloc of six Arab Gulf monarchies alarmed by the Iranian Revolution and the Iran-Iraq War raging next door.

Iraq began attacking Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, and Iran retaliated against ships serving Arab Gulf states, turning commercial shipping lanes into a war zone in what became known as the Tanker War.

The US Navy launched Operation Earnest Will, reflagging Kuwaiti tankers under the American flag and escorting them through the Strait of Hormuz — the first direct US military commitment to keeping the strait open by force.

The USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the strait, killing all 290 civilians aboard including 66 children; the US never formally apologized and awarded the ship's captain a Legion of Merit.

Operation Praying Mantis saw the US Navy sink or cripple half of Iran's operational fleet in a single day — the largest American naval engagement since World War II and a lesson Tehran has never forgotten about conventional confrontation with Washington.

George W. Bush named Iran part of an 'Axis of Evil' alongside Iraq and North Korea, collapsing a brief post-9/11 period of US-Iran cooperation on Afghanistan and convincing Tehran's hardliners that Washington would never accept the Islamic Republic's existence.

Iran reportedly sent a comprehensive negotiation proposal to Washington through the Swiss embassy offering concessions on nuclear development, Hezbollah, and Hamas; the Bush administration ignored it.
The Stuxnet worm, jointly developed by the US and Israel, destroyed roughly 1,000 Iranian centrifuges — the first known cyberweapon deployed to physically sabotage another country's infrastructure.

Iran and the P5+1 signed the JCPOA in Vienna, trading strict nuclear limits for sanctions relief in a deal that took 20 months of negotiation and was considered the most significant US-Iran diplomatic achievement since the revolution.
Trump unilaterally withdrew the US from the JCPOA despite Iran's verified compliance, reimposing crippling sanctions and destroying the diplomatic framework that had taken two decades to build.

A US drone strike at Baghdad airport killed Qasem Soleimani, commander of Iran's Quds Force and arguably the second most powerful figure in the Islamic Republic — the most provocative US escalation against Iran since 1988.

Israel assassinated Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, Iran's top nuclear scientist, on a highway outside Tehran using a remote-controlled machine gun — the latest in a string of targeted killings of Iranian nuclear personnel.
China brokered a surprise restoration of Saudi-Iranian diplomatic relations after seven years of rupture, signaling that Gulf security architecture was no longer Washington's exclusive domain.

Iran launched its first-ever direct military strike on Israeli territory, firing over 300 drones and missiles in retaliation for Israel's bombing of the Iranian consulate in Damascus — crossing a threshold both countries had avoided for 45 years.

The Strait of Hormuz narrows to just 24 miles at its tightest point between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of global oil shipments and one-third of seaborne liquefied natural gas pass through it daily, making it the single most consequential chokepoint in the global economy.

iran-us-israel-war.label: Iran-US-Israel war: Gulf states weigh military entry, Hormuz blockade tightens

timeline.body: Congress passed the Posse Comitatus Act after Reconstruction, barring federal military forces from enforcing domestic law — a line that would blur two centuries later as immigration agents took on quasi-military roles inside civilian spaces.
Air traffic controllers formed PATCO, the first major union of federal aviation workers, asserting that the people who keep planes from colliding deserve collective bargaining power.

Ronald Reagan fired 11,345 striking air traffic controllers and decertified their union, establishing the precedent that federal workers who keep the skies running can be treated as disposable when they assert their rights.

The first major modern government shutdown lasted 21 days after President Clinton and Speaker Gingrich deadlocked over the federal budget, normalizing the idea that Congress could hold government services hostage to political leverage.

Before September 11, airport security was handled by private contractors paid near minimum wage — the 19 hijackers passed through checkpoints staffed by undertrained, underpaid screeners with no federal oversight.

Congress passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act 69 days after 9/11, federalizing airport security and creating the TSA with 55,000 employees, the largest expansion of the federal workforce since the Post Office.
The Homeland Security Act merged 22 separate agencies into the Department of Homeland Security, the biggest federal reorganization since the Department of Defense was created in 1947.

ICE absorbed the functions of the old Immigration and Naturalization Service and U.S. Customs Service, combining immigration enforcement and criminal investigation under one roof with minimal congressional oversight of its evolving mission.

A 16-day government shutdown furloughed 800,000 federal workers, but TSA agents were classified as 'essential' — meaning they were legally required to keep showing up without any guarantee of when they would be paid.

The longest shutdown in U.S. history stretched 35 days over border wall funding, forcing 51,000 TSA officers to screen passengers without paychecks while members of Congress continued collecting their salaries.

TSA sickout rates hit 10% during the 35-day shutdown as unpaid agents simply stopped coming to work, causing hourslong security lines at major airports and proving that the entire air travel system depends on workers the government treats as expendable.

The Federal Employees Fair Treatment Act guaranteed back pay for essential workers after shutdowns, but did nothing to prevent them from going weeks without income in the first place — no paycheck, just a promise.

ICE expanded its presence at domestic airports under the Trump administration, conducting enforcement operations at terminals and gates — spaces previously reserved for TSA's transportation security mission.

Delta Air Lines operated a Congressional VIP escort program at major airports, a perk so routine that most travelers never knew their elected officials were fast-tracked past the same security lines they fund and sometimes shut down.

TSA officers earn a median salary of roughly $47,000 — significantly less than other federal law enforcement — and were excluded from the standard federal pay scale until 2023, when Congress finally granted them the same system other agencies had from the start.
Unlike military personnel, who receive pay during shutdowns through separate appropriations, TSA and other DHS employees depend on annual funding bills that Congress routinely fails to pass on time.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports
